title: The Progress of EdTech Depends on Our Tolerance for Error
author: Becky Allen
summary: Prompted by a teacher's post about a faulty chemistry question on a school platform, Allen argues that EdTech progress is stalled by an expectation of zero error from AI tools that we never apply to textbooks, exams or teachers. Borrowing Karpathy's idea of the march of nines, she notes that LLMs reach roughly 90 percent reliability easily but each further nine is brutal, so demanding perfection means shipping nothing. Her move is to shift the question from whether the AI erred to what ecosystem makes an error survivable. She describes seeding new items among well-understood ones, tracking whether stronger students succeed more, capping exposure, and A/B testing explanations against trusted anchors. She extends the idea to high-stakes assessment through on-demand tests built on large LLM-generated item banks, where errors surface in low-stakes settings and small numbers. The conclusion is to tolerate tiny contained mistakes while preventing mass ones.
points: The real obstacle to AI in classrooms is an unreachable zero-error standard that is not applied to human-made materials; the difference is exposure, since platform errors reach thousands.
The march of nines explains why LLM demos impress while the last few percent of reliability are very costly.
Errors can be policed by mixing new items among known ones, monitoring whether stronger students do better, and pausing items that behave oddly.
Instructional errors can be detected with anchor questions, A/B tests against the current best explanation and early signals such as time-on-task and help requests.
LLM-generated item banks could support unique on-demand public assessments, with test takers quietly validating a few seed items.
quotes: But the moment an error pops up in front of real pupils, our tolerance collapses; we expect zero wrongness from software in a way we don’t from textbooks, exam papers, or (let’s be honest) ourselves.
Using LLMs in EdTech feels the same. With careful prompts, they already achieve the first nine of marking or explanation: they are helpful about 90% of the time. That’s why the demos wow us.
Right now we hold AI to a zero-error bar where humans routinely slip, and that stalls the inner-loop feedback we want. Why tolerate teacher errors but not LLM errors? Exposure.

Mix a small number of new items among well-understood ones so you already know roughly how capable each student is in that topic. As answers come in, the system keeps a running estimate of whether the new item behaves like it should: do stronger students get it right more often than weaker ones?

If not, you cap exposure (only dozens see it, not thousands), pull the item for review, and fix or replace it. Think of it as smoke detectors for questions: a few odd readings and the alarm goes off before anyone gets hurt.

To do that, you need a question bank large enough that memorisation is futile, i.e. you have to understand the subject matter to pass. That’s exactly where LLMs excel: generating vast, varied item pools across subjects.

The way forward is to design for the march of nines: tolerate tiny, contained mistakes; instrument everything; cap exposure; fix fast. That’s how we protect trust and finally deliver the inner-loop feedback tools we’ve been promised.
